body: A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold. Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing. The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, nearly twice the 8% decline economists had expected, as lending to property investors collapsed in the wake of government tax changes and a year of Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes. Investor lending was the main drag, plunging 32.3% on the quarter after a 10.2% fall in the June quarter. Owner-occupier loan values fell a more modest 5.3%, following a 1.9% decline previously. The overall drop was a sharp acceleration from the 5.2% fall recorded in the prior quarter. The split between investors and owner-occupiers suggests policy is doing much of the work. In the May federal budget, the government moved to end negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night, keeping it only for newly built properties, and also announced curbs to the capital gains tax discount on established dwellings. Negative gearing lets investors offset rental losses against other income. The government argued the housing market needed rebalancing, with most investor credit going towards existing homes rather than new supply. The major banks moved quickly to reflect the changes in how they assess investor loan applications, reducing borrowing capacity for many landlords. Those measures came on top of tighter lending rules. From February, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority required banks to limit new loans at six or more times a borrower’s income to 20% of new mortgage lending, measured separately for owner-occupiers and investors. Monetary policy has added further pressure. The RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, in February, March, May, September and November, taking it to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, as it fights inflation that has been pushed higher by energy costs. The November decision was split 6-3, and the statement dropped earlier language about further increases. The RBA’s own November Statement on Monetary Policy had already flagged a steep fall in investor lending, describing the drop in investor loan commitments as the largest in any hiking cycle on record. Governor Michele Bullock said a pullback in investor demand was normal in a housing downturn. The bigger fall compared with owner-occupiers, though, suggests the budget changes are having an effect. The figures strengthen the case that housing is cooling quickly, which may feed into the RBA’s assessment of whether its tightening has gone far enough. body: The broad-based jump in confidence, especially among service firms, adds to the picture of a Japanese economy strong enough to cope with higher interest rates. Combined with the reported tight labour market and persistent cost pressure, that could support expectations of further Bank of Japan tightening, which would be supportive for the yen. For equities, the strength in electronics and precision machinery reinforces the chip-led earnings story behind Japan’s tech and equipment names. The caution on passing costs on to customers is a reminder that margin pressure has not gone away. Japan Inc’s mood is at multi-year highs on chips and services, even as rising prices and borrowing costs start to pinch. Japanese manufacturers’ confidence climbed to its highest level in more than five years in November, lifted by booming semiconductor demand, while sentiment among non-manufacturers reached its strongest in over eight years, according to the Reuters Tankan poll. The manufacturers’ index rose to +27 from +22 in October, its highest reading since August 2021. The non-manufacturers’ index surged to +35 from +23, a level last seen in June 2018. The monthly poll is closely watched as a leading indicator for the Bank of Japan’s quarterly Tankan business survey. It was conducted from October 27 to November 6, and 214 of the 508 firms surveyed responded. Readings are calculated by subtracting the percentage of pessimistic responses from optimistic ones, so a positive figure signals net optimism. Chipmakers and their suppliers drove the gain among manufacturers. Sentiment in electronics jumped to +39 from +25, with one respondent describing demand for semiconductors, particularly memory chips, as very strong. Precision machinery, which includes some chip equipment makers, improved to +42 from +38 on robust domestic and overseas orders. Another machinery firm said shipments to the semiconductor market had reached unprecedented levels. Oil refining and ceramics rose to +25 from +14, while chemicals improved to +33 from +27. The service side of the economy was just as upbeat. Information and communications sentiment rose to +29 from +8 on strong orders, while services and others more than doubled to +43 from +19. One manager pointed to persistently tight labour market conditions keeping demand for staff high. Not everything was positive. Firms in both sectors said rising prices and higher interest rates were weighing on business, and some reported difficulty passing increased costs on to customers. Looking ahead, manufacturers expect sentiment to edge up to +28 in February, while non-manufacturers see confidence easing to +29, still well above recent levels. For the Bank of Japan, the combination of strong business confidence, a tight labour market and cost pressures will be one input as it weighs the outlook for policy. Its own quarterly Tankan will be the next major read on corporate sentiment. There's always something new to learn about the markets. Middle Eastern benchmarks have been weakening for weeks, suggesting an oil glut may be building amid rebounding Persian Gulf exports and global demand destruction amid high prices. On the face of it, an oversupply of crude oil could be forming. But the costs to refiners and consumers are not falling. War, insurance premiums, and record tanker rates have raised the cost of transporting a barrel of crude oil from about $5 per barrel before the war to as much as $30 a barrel, and at times even higher. Middle Eastern producers are forced to slash their official selling prices to win customers because the surge in Persian Gulf exports is weakening the physical prices of local grades. Moreover, amid high freight costs, Middle East’s crude oil could only win Asia’s price-sensitive buyers with lower prices. The pricing of the Middle Eastern barrels and the weakening market structure of the benchmark Middle East crudes signal an oil glut is forming. But the shock to the global oil and fuel markets isn’t over as increased flows don’t mean traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has suddenly become less dangerous. In fact, attacks on vessels have intensified in the past month, while producers are tying up a large portion of the global tanker fleet on inefficient shuttle movements in and out of the Strait and subsequent ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Normal oil trade patterns from before the Iran war may never return. Until the market adapts to the new normal and Gulf producers build alternative supply routes, the war and insurance premium risks will remain with crude flows. South Sudan is courting fresh capital for 14 exploration blocks and a production increase from roughly 170,000 barrels per day to 230,000, which investors would find impossible to control once those barrels left the country. Captive to neighboring Sudan’s civil war, South Sudan is essentially divvying up its oil, under duress, between the Sudanese Army and the rival paramilitary RSF, which extract payment before the oil can reach the Red Sea. The government-backed South Sudan Oil & Power conference will put that proposition before investors in Juba at the end of the month, and its organizers place current production at 170,000 barrels per day, describing 230,000 bpd as a short-term target. A petroleum ministry official reported production of 175,000 bpd in August and set a lower target of 200,000 bpd by August 2027. Tanker tracking recorded eight cargoes carrying 4.8 million barrels from Sudan’s two Red Sea terminals in October, equivalent to combined Sudanese and South Sudanese exports of 155,000 bpd . Sudan’s Heglig fields were producing about 26,000 bpd in September, all of it sent for export, according to Sudan Tribune . Public data provide no current country breakdown and no reconciliation between South Sudan’s reported wellhead production and the volumes loaded at the Red Sea terminals. Juba’s lofty ambitions in the middle of the civil war in Sudan, which has effectively hijacked its exports, are an attempt to ride the tailwinds of the launch of the Africa Energy Bank. Afreximbank and the African Petroleum Producers’ Organisation formally established the institution in Abuja on October 31 with $5 billion in authorized capital . APPO Secretary-General Farid Ghezali said the bank had raised $500 million for deployment and would begin making investment decisions. Fresh capital can finance production inside South Sudan, but it can’t secure passage through Sudan. Crude from Blocks 1, 2 and 4 enters the Greater Nile pipeline through Heglig in West Kordofan, where Sudan’s paramilitary RSF displaced the Sudanese Army in December 2025. A tripartite agreement placed security inside the complex with the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces. South Sudanese troops now protect the installation, while the RSF dominates the surrounding territory and the Sudanese Army controls the Red Sea terminals at the other end of the line. A September report citing unnamed oil-industry sources says Juba gives the RSF $4 of the $11 charged on each South Sudanese barrel crossing territory under its control. The army-aligned government receives the remaining $7. South Sudan has previously settled pipeline obligations with crude , although no published account identifies whether the RSF’s current share is delivered in oil, cash or export proceeds. The Army’s portion provides more than compensation for operating a pipeline. Janes assesses that Sudanese processing and transit fees provide revenue used to sustain Army operations. The RSF collects its share in exchange for allowing the crude to cross territory it controls. Investors financing production connected to Heglig would add barrels to a trade that pays both forces. South Sudan’s second export line avoids Heglig, but doesn’t escape the war. The Petrodar pipeline carries Dar Blend from Blocks 3 and 7 at Paloch through six pumping stations in Sudan to the Bashair terminal on the Red Sea. COP 31, the latest iteration of the United Nations’ annual climate conference, kicked off today in Antalya, Türkiye, and achieving 35 percent global electrification by 2035 is going to be one of the event’s most central agenda items. Until extremely recently, this target likely would have seemed overly ambitious, but experts say that a number of factors, including volatile oil and gas markets stemming from the war in Iran, paired with enormous advances in clean energy technologies, have now put that goal within “striking distance.” All of that electrification is going to require a whole lot of lithium. Over the course of this decade alone, lithium demand has already skyrocketed by more than 400 percent on a global scale to top 1.5 million metric tons per year. Projecting out to 2035, the year featured in COP 31’s proposed electrification pledge, global demand could reach approximately 4 million tons. In the International Energy Agency’s Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 , no mineral is expected to see bigger demand growth. This is leading to increased competition over global lithium supply chains as nations rush to shore up their own future supplies to ensure long-term energy security in a rapidly changing energy landscape. But even as a diverse array of countries try to establish homegrown lithium production and refining sectors, one nation is expected to maintain an extreme degree of control over global supplies: China. Beijing controls an estimated 72 percent of the global lithium-ion market, and Chinese companies control a quarter of the world’s lithium mining capacity . This control runs up the supply chain as well: in 2024, more than 80 percent of battery cells on the planet were made in China, raising major concerns about geopolitical precarity and market resilience in clean energy supply chains. By 2030, Beijing is expected to control 39 percent of the world’s lithium production, according to a recent report from Wood Mackenzie. “Lithium production and lithium ownership are increasingly diverging, and it is reshaping the global critical mineral supply chains,” said Allan Pedersen, research director, energy transition & battery materials – lithium at Wood Mackenzie. “While production growth is becoming more geographically diverse, ownership remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies, mostly led by China.” By comparison, the United States produces just barely over 1 percent of the world’s lithium supplies, a large share of which comes from a single mine: Albemarle’s Silver Peak mine in Nevada. body: API Shows Sharp Build in US Crude Oil, Distillate Inventories Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated that crude oil inventories in the United States rose by 9.0 million barrels in the week ending November 6. In the week prior, US crude oil inventories fell by 5.267 million barrels. Commercial crude oil inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 54 million barrels over the last 30 weeks, and 3 million over this year, according to API data, which has been kept in check in part thanks to draws from the SPR. For the week ending November 6, 2.7 million barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 279.5 million barrels —a level that is 434 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. The generally accepted operational minimum for oil in the SPR is between 250-300 million barrels, below which the reserve may find it difficult to pump and process oil efficiently. title: American Barrick files for proposed IPO
summary: Barrick Mining announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation.
body: Barrick Mining (NYSE:B)(TSX:ABX) announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company, which will hold Barrick’s North American gold assets, will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation. The world’s third-biggest gold miner said it is moving forward with the proposed initial public offering (IPO) and has filed a registration statement on Form S-11 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in connection with the proposed IPO. American Barrick intends to apply to list its common stock on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol ‘ABGC’. The number of shares to be offered and the proposed price range for the IPO have not yet been determined, the company said, adding that net proceeds from the IPO will be distributed to Barrick, which it expects to return to its shareholders. In September, chief executive officer Mark Hill said the planned North American gold IPO could slip into January. Hill, who was named in August to lead the North American unit after it goes public, said there had been “some delays” in working through formalities ahead of the listing. Barrick first announced last year its proposal to hive off its US assets from its sprawling portfolio in riskier countries. The new company will house Barrick’s joint-venture interests and the Fourmile discovery in the state of Nevada, which it has touted as “one of the century’s greatest gold discoveries.” Barrick struck a deal with Newmont in August that gave the Denver-based company a stake in Fourmile and brought the deposit into the joint Nevada Gold Mines venture in exchange for support of the planned IPO. This is reflected in technical analysis of oil price movements. Technical analysts use historical price charts to forecast market direction. One indicator they monitor in a declining market is the support level, which represents a price threshold that could act as a floor against further declines. Previous highs and lows often serve as support areas. Moving averages also play a role, smoothing out the impact of extreme fluctuations to reveal the underlying market trend. In addition, analysts use Fibonacci retracement, a percentage-based calculation to identify price levels that markets often retest after a particular move. One key Fibonacci level is now serving as a reference point for global oil prices, tracked through Brent crude futures contracts. The recent decline in oil prices briefly stalled around the 50% retracement level of the rally from July to October. According to LSEG data, this level stands at USD 94.07 per barrel and has now become an important support area. The level is also reinforced by the 200-day moving average at around USD 93.84 and the 40-week moving average at USD 95.27. After a sharp decline, markets typically pause to digest the move. This is known as consolidation and is often viewed as a healthy development within a trend. To assess the likelihood of further market declines, technical analysts use several momentum and volatility indicators. One is the Relative Strength Index (RSI), which measures momentum based on the duration and magnitude of price movements. Another is the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), which compares two moving averages to measure momentum. Analysts also use Bollinger Bands, which measure price deviations from a central moving average to gauge volatility. But the company, seen as the leader of the "neocloud" pack, has seen roughly 65% of its market value evaporate from its high six months ago, and the strong numbers clearly failed to dispel market doubts. The real pressure comes from three ropes tightening at once: rising political resistance to data center construction after the midterm elections, largest customer Microsoft tightening oversight of some projects, and the debt burden reflected in corporate bond yields that have surged past 15%. According to figures released by the company, CoreWeave's third-quarter revenue was $3.66 billion (about NT$120 billion), above the $3.55 billion market estimate. Its per-share loss of $0.95 was also better than the $1.16 loss analysts expected. The company raised its 2026 full-year revenue forecast to $13 billion to $13.3 billion (about NT$440 billion) from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion, and lifted its adjusted operating income forecast to $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion from $960 million to $1.15 billion. The order metric drew even more attention. As of the end of September, signed but unrecognized revenue had climbed to $132.5 billion (about NT$4.4 trillion) from $104 billion at the end of June, an increase of $28.5 billion in just one quarter. The figure, seen as a gauge of future sales visibility, shows customer purchases of AI compute are still expanding. Note: Figures are as disclosed in the company's third-quarter earnings report, denominated in U.S. dollars. Yet the flip side of the order surge is ballooning capital expenditure. CoreWeave's third-quarter capex jumped to $14.5 billion from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter, and the company raised the low end of its full-year spending range by another $2 billion, to a latest forecast of $37 billion to $39 billion (about NT$1.3 trillion). Data centers must be built and GPUs procured before the company can start charging customers for compute, and the massive investment typically precedes revenue recovery, making funding schedules the most fragile link in the expansion process. As of the end of September, the company's total debt stood at about $46.9 billion (about NT$1.5 trillion), while adjusted profitability is not expected until the first half of 2028. CEO Mike Intrator stressed that the company follows a "secure customer contracts first, then invest in construction" model rather than building compute capacity and then looking for customers, and that customers typically share part of the construction cost. He also said the company expects to receive $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, and that with the market currently demanding higher yields, there is no need to issue unsecured bonds to raise funds. The immediate trigger for market sentiment was the election outcome. Voters in many localities came out clearly against building data centers near residential communities, boosting the influence of state and local governments that take a more conservative stance on AI infrastructure. In Texas, for example, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has publicly called for an immediate pause on data center project approvals, and CoreWeave promptly sent a letter expressing its willingness to seek cooperation.
